authorities.cite: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 120-2-52-.06 (Total Loss Vehicle Claims)
authorities.text_quote: the insurer may elect to pay a cash equivalent settlement based upon the actual cost less any deductible provided in the policy, to purchase a comparable automobile by the same manufacturer, same model year, with similar body style, similar options and mileage, including all applicable taxes, license fees and other fees incident to the transfer of ownership of a comparable automobile.
authorities.verified_how: curl of Cornell LII rule page 2026-10-05 (rules.sos.ga.gov refuses TLS from this network; sibling packs cite https://rules.sos.ga.gov/gac/120-2-52). Valuation sources: 2+ comparables within 50 miles of the county seat where garaged (then 100 miles), dealer quotes, or a statistically valid database. Taxes/fees capped at what the totaled vehicle would have paid. Contains NO total-loss percentage threshold and NO requirement to give the insured a written ACV explanation.

replacements.old_exact: Both Georgia and South Carolina use a threshold based on a percentage of the vehicle's ACV, though the specific percentages and regulatory frameworks differ.
replacements.new_text: South Carolina sets that line by statute at 75% of fair market value; Georgia sets no percentage and leaves the call to the insurer.
replacements.note: Georgia has no percentage threshold anywhere in statute or rule.

replacements.old_exact: Georgia regulates total loss vehicle claims under O.C.G.A. § 33-34-6. Under Georgia law, an insurer must declare a vehicle a total loss when the cost of repairs exceeds the vehicle's fair market value. Georgia does not set a hard statutory percentage threshold; instead, insurers apply their own internal thresholds, typically between 75% and 100% of ACV depending on the company.
replacements.new_text: Georgia's total loss settlement rules are in Insurance Commissioner Rule 120-2-52-.06, which covers claims under your own policy. Georgia law sets no total loss threshold; the insurer decides when repair no longer makes economic sense.
replacements.note: § 33-34-6 is the repair-shop-choice statute. No GA law requires a total loss when repairs exceed FMV. '75%-100%' internal thresholds is unsourced; dropped.

replacements.old_exact: Georgia does mandate transparency. The insurer must provide a written explanation of how the ACV was calculated, including the comparable vehicles used. If you disagree, you have the right to obtain an independent appraisal.
replacements.new_text: The rule requires a cash settlement to cover a comparable vehicle — same make and model year, similar options and mileage — plus taxes, license and transfer fees. If you disagree, you can invoke your policy's appraisal clause.
replacements.note: Rule has no written-explanation duty. Taxes/fees capped at what the totaled vehicle would have paid. Appraisal right is contractual (policy), not statutory.

replacements.old_exact: Once a vehicle is declared a total loss in Georgia, the title must be branded as "salvage" through the Georgia Department of Revenue's Motor Vehicle Division. If the vehicle is later rebuilt to meet safety inspection standards, it can receive a "rebuilt" title — but the salvage history remains permanent. Rebuilt vehicles must pass a state inspection before re-registration,
replacements.new_text: Once an insurer pays a total loss claim in Georgia, the vehicle needs a salvage title from the Department of Revenue unless the damage is only cosmetic and not from fire or flood (O.C.G.A. §§ 40-3-2, 40-3-36). If it is rebuilt, the Department inspects the VIN, the bills of sale for major parts and the required safety equipment before issuing a title marked "rebuilt" (§ 40-3-37),
replacements.note: Sentence continues with the existing 'and a rebuilt title typically reduces resale value by 20% to 40%.' — that figure is unsourced and outside this legal-framework scope; flag for the refresher.

replacements.old_exact: South Carolina addresses total loss vehicles through S.C. Code § 38-77-30 and related insurance regulations. South Carolina law requires insurers to act in good faith when evaluating total loss claims, and the state's Department of Insurance actively regulates how these valuations are conducted.
replacements.new_text: South Carolina defines a total loss by statute: a vehicle whose repair cost, parts and labor, equals or exceeds 75% of its pre-loss fair market value (S.C. Code § 56-19-480(G)). Lowball settlement as a general business practice is an improper claim practice the Department of Insurance polices (§ 38-59-20).
replacements.note: § 38-77-30 is the auto-insurance definitions section. SC has no total-loss valuation regulation (Chapter 69 checked). § 38-59-20 needs a 'general business practice' and gives no private remedy.

replacements.old_exact: In South Carolina, most insurers use a total loss threshold of approximately 75% of ACV, meaning that if repair costs reach 75% of the vehicle's pre-accident value, the insurer will declare it a total loss rather than authorize repairs. However, the exact threshold varies by insurer and policy terms.
replacements.new_text: In practice, a vehicle with damage of 75% or more of its pre-accident value must be declared a total loss, and an insurer may also total a car below that line. Vehicles worth $2,000 or less and antiques fall outside the statute.
replacements.note: The 75% is statutory/SCDMV-mandated, not an insurer custom.

replacements.old_exact: When a South Carolina insurer declares a vehicle a total loss, the insurer must obtain the title and submit a salvage certificate to the SC Department of Motor Vehicles. If the vehicle is later rebuilt, the owner must obtain a rebuilt title by passing an anti-theft inspection conducted by the State Law Enforcement Division (SLED). This inspection confirms VIN accuracy, verifies no stolen parts were used, and checks that the vehicle is safe to operate. As in Georgia, a rebuilt title permanently marks the vehicle's history and reduces market value.
replacements.new_text: When a South Carolina insurer declares a vehicle a total loss — whether it takes the car or leaves it with you — it must send the title and a damage report to the SC Department of Motor Vehicles, which brands the title salvage (S.C. Code § 56-19-480(B)). To retitle a rebuilt vehicle, the owner files an application listing the source and cost of parts and the repairs done, and the title is marked "salvage rebuilt" (§ 56-19-480(E)). The salvage brand can never be removed.
replacements.note: No SLED inspection exists in Title 56 Ch. 19 or SCDMV's total-loss guidance; the SLED claim is dropped. (A secondary source suggests SCDMV 'may' require an officer inspection; not found in current § 56-19-480 text — do not assert either way.)
